newsitem.title: USA: Diane Sawyer defends use of hidden cameras. [CORRECTED 09:10 GMT 11/1]
newsitem.headline: Diane Sawyer defends use of hidden cameras. [CORRECTED 09:10 GMT 11/1]

text.p: Star co-anchor Diane Sawyer of ABC's PrimeTime Live programme on Friday defended the use of hidden cameras in news reporting, even though they can be seen as deceptive.

"It is a rare and important thing to be able to see it (an incident) for yourself," she testified in Food Lion Inc.'s lawsuit against Walt Disney Co.'s ABC over the network's hidden-camera investigation of its stores.

ABC lost a civil suit late last year in which Food Lion charged it with fraud, trespass and breach of loyalty when two ABC producers used hidden cameras in a 1992 television report about the grocery store chain's sanitation and food-handling practices. (Corrects to make clear that ABC lost a civil suit).

Sawyer said she was aware that the report would be a hidden camera investigation. "My understanding was that it would be completely legal," she said. "It was clear that the questions being raised were serious questions about the buying of food you bring home to your family."
Sawyer testified only briefly in U.S. District Court, where jurors were hearing evidence in the punitive-damages phase of the trial.

The jury had previously awarded Food Lion $1,400 in compensatory damages. Food Lion, a unit of Belgian retailer ETS Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION" SA, reportedly is seeking up to $2 billion in punitive damages.

When asked whether she agreed that hidden camera interviews boosted television ratings, Sawyer said she believed that interest in a person, issue or the immediacy of an issue dictated interest in a programme.

She cited examples including her widely watched interview with the basketball star Magic Johnson, who retired from the Los Angeles Lakers after learning he was HIV positive, rejoined the team and then retired again after some players objected to his return.
Sawyer left the stand at mid-afternoon after a short cross examination.
